justice: Both sides of the bridge provide raised sidewalks separated from the carriageway, so pedestrian space is not entirely sacrificed to motor traffic.
The roadway is much wider than the pedestrian realm, with multiple vehicle lanes and only narrow side paths, indicating an uneven distribution of space among travel modes.
Short black-and-yellow bollards protect the right sidewalk edge from vehicle encroachment, but they also narrow usable edge space and may complicate passing in constrained sections.
No visible tactile paving, marked curb ramps, or dedicated crossing facilities can be identified in the image, limiting inclusive accessibility for a full range of users.
safety: The sidewalks are vertically separated from the road by curbs, reducing direct conflict between pedestrians and moving vehicles.
Tall streetlights are installed along the bridge, which likely improves nighttime visibility and perceived security.
The bridge alignment is straight and sightlines are long, helping drivers detect other users well in advance.
There is no visible protected bicycle lane or clear cycling space, creating potential mixing risk for cyclists on a relatively fast road.
The wide open roadway and bridge setting may encourage higher vehicle speeds, which can reduce safety despite low visible traffic.
livability: The setting is a bridge corridor with little visible active frontage, shops, seating, or social destinations, so everyday street life appears limited.
There are no visible benches, shelters, kiosks, or public gathering elements on either sidewalk, reducing stay activity and social use.
Green tree canopies are visible beyond and beside the bridge, which improves environmental quality compared with a fully hardscaped corridor.
The scene appears clean and uncluttered, but its transport-oriented design offers few amenities that support lingering, recreation, or community interaction.
sustainability: The substantial tree cover visible along the sides of the bridge contributes to urban greenery and ecological value.
Street lighting infrastructure may support efficient public-space use, but no renewable energy features or water-sensitive design elements are visible.
No dedicated bus stop, transit stop, or obvious multimodal interchange is visible in the image, limiting evidence of sustainable transport support.
The absence of a marked bicycle facility weakens support for low-carbon cycling trips across the bridge.
aesthetics: The bridge has a clean, orderly appearance with consistent white lamp poles and regular railing design, creating strong visual coherence.
Open sky views and the long perspective across the bridge give the scene a spacious and visually pleasant character.
The surrounding greenery softens the hard infrastructure and adds natural color contrast to the roadway and sidewalks.
The environment appears well maintained, with neat pavement surfaces and minimal visible litter or visual clutter.
comfort: The sidewalks appear smooth, wide enough for basic walking, and largely free of clutter, supporting physical comfort for pedestrians.
Tree shade is concentrated mostly at the right edge of the foreground, while much of the bridge deck and sidewalks are exposed to direct sun, reducing thermal comfort.
No benches, shelters, or resting points are visible along the bridge, limiting comfort for users who need pauses during longer trips.
Low visible traffic and the open setting likely reduce crowding stress, supporting better psychological comfort than a busy urban street.
walkability: Continuous sidewalks are provided on both sides of the bridge, allowing pedestrians to traverse the corridor without stepping into traffic.
The bridge environment is dedicated mainly to movement, with no visible crossings, destinations, or active edges that would make walking more attractive or practical.
Direct sun exposure over most of the bridge and the lack of seating reduce walking comfort, especially for longer distances.
Protective railings and curb separation improve basic walking security, but the overall scale remains strongly vehicle-oriented.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycle markings, or physically protected cycling track is visible on the bridge.
Cyclists would likely need to share space either with motor vehicles in general lanes or with pedestrians on the sidewalks, both of which reduce cycling quality.
The wide, straight roadway provides good forward visibility, which helps basic riding conditions, but does not compensate for lack of dedicated infrastructure.
No bicycle parking, bike signals, or cycle-specific wayfinding elements are visible, indicating weak support for cycling use.
